t: Notwithstanding any other provision of this title, no patient shall be committed to a hospital of the Service under this title if the Surgeon General certifies that adequate facilities or personnel for treatment of such patient are unavailable.

fable.w: The only decision-maker here is the Surgeon General, a federal official, who certifies on his own that facilities or personnel are unavailable. A reader might be tempted to treat the certification or the commitment process as procedural participation, but the section provides no consultation, hearing, comment process, advisory body, or right to sue for anyone outside the federal government. It is simply a limit on committing patients to Service hospitals.
fable.s: the Surgeon General certifies that adequate facilities or personnel for treatment of such patient are unavailable

qwen_block.w: This section establishes a condition for committing a patient based on a certification by the Surgeon General, a federal official. It does not involve consultation with or participation by any party outside the federal government (such as the public, states, or private entities). The decision-making process described is entirely internal to the federal government.
qwen_block.s: Notwithstanding any other provision of this title, no patient shall be committed to a hospital of the Service under this title if the Surgeon General certifies that adequate facilities or personnel for treatment of such patient are unavailable.

opus.w: The only decision here is the Surgeon General's own certification that facilities or staff are unavailable, and that decision stays entirely inside the federal government. The word "committed" might suggest a court proceeding, but this section creates no hearing, consultation, advisory body, or right to sue for anyone outside the government.
opus.s: no patient shall be committed to a hospital of the Service under this title if the Surgeon General certifies that adequate facilities or personnel for treatment of such patient are unavailable
opus.b: The tempting reading is that "committed" suggests a court commitment proceeding, which would involve outside parties. That doesn't hold up. The section only lets the Surgeon General, a federal official, certify that facilities or staff aren't available. No outside party is consulted, there is no hearing or comment period, and no one is given a right to object or sue.
